problem: 'demanded' softened to 'requested'; 'connived at' rendered 'went along with' (connive = tolerate, not join).
replacement: In all the confederations formed before the American Union, the Federal government demanded its supplies from the separate governments. If the measure it prescribed was burdensome to any one of those bodies, ways were found to evade its claims. A powerful State resorted to arms; a weak one tolerated the resistance that the law of the Union, its sovereign, met with, and fell back on inaction under the excuse of inability. In these circumstances one of two outcomes has invariably occurred. Either the most dominant of the allied peoples has taken over the privileges of the Federal authority and ruled all the States in its name, *p or the Federal government has been abandoned by its natural supporters, anarchy has arisen among the confederates, and the Union has lost all power to act. *q

problem: General statement ('When several nations form...') turned into a hypothetical ('Suppose').
replacement: The human mind invents new things more easily than new words, and so we are forced to use a multitude of improper and inadequate expressions. When several nations form a permanent league and establish a supreme authority, which does not have the same influence over the members of the community as a national government but acts on each of the Confederate States as a whole, this government, so essentially different from all others, is called a Federal one. Later another form of society is discovered, in which several peoples are fused into one and the same nation with regard to certain common interests, while they remain distinct, or at least only confederate, with regard to all their other concerns. In this case the central power acts directly on those it governs, rules, and judges, in the same manner as a national government but within a more limited sphere. Here the term Federal government clearly no longer applies to a state of things that must be called an incomplete national government. A form of government has been found that is neither exactly national nor federal. But no further progress has been made, and the new word that will one day name this new invention does not yet exist.

problem: Added connective 'therefore' that is not in the source.
replacement: But the Confederate States of America had long been accustomed to forming part of one empire before they won their independence. They had not acquired the habit of governing themselves, and their national prejudices had not taken deep root in their minds. Superior to the rest of the world in political knowledge, and sharing that knowledge equally among themselves, they were little troubled by the passions that generally oppose the extension of federal authority in a nation, and the wisdom of the leading citizens kept those passions in check. The Americans applied the remedy with prudent firmness as soon as they became aware of the evil. They amended their laws, and they saved their country.

problem: 'abstract of provincial patriotism' rendered 'sum', which suggests aggregation rather than epitome.
replacement: Happiness and freedom of small nations — Power of great nations — Great empires favorable to the growth of civilization — Strength is often the first element of national prosperity — The aim of the Federal system is to unite the twofold advantages of a small and a large territory — Advantages the United States has gained from this system — The law adapts itself to the needs of the population; the population does not conform to the needs of the law — Activity, improvement, and love and enjoyment of freedom in the American communities — The public spirit of the Union is the summary of provincial patriotism — Principles and things circulate freely over the territory of the United States — The Union is happy and free like a small nation, and respected like a great empire.

problem: 'manners' (mores) left as 'manners'; STYLE-NOTE requires 'customs' where the whole set of habits is meant.
replacement: In small nations the scrutiny of society reaches into every part, and the spirit of improvement enters into the smallest details. The ambition of the people is necessarily held in check by its weakness, so all the efforts and resources of the citizens are turned to the internal benefit of the community and are not likely to vanish in the fleeting breath of glory. The desires of every individual are limited, because extraordinary abilities are rarely found. The gifts of an equal fortune make the various conditions of life uniform, and the customs of the inhabitants are orderly and simple. So if we weigh the degrees of popular morality and education, we shall generally find that small nations have more people in easy circumstances, a more numerous population, and a more tranquil society than great empires do.

problem: 'censure the imprudence' strengthened to 'condemn the rashness'.
replacement: No great nation in the history of the world has kept a republican form of government for a long series of years, *r and this has led people to conclude that such a thing is impracticable. For my part, I cannot help blaming the imprudence of a being who tries to limit the possible and to judge the future. He is deceived every hour by the most obvious realities of life, and he is constantly taken by surprise in the circumstances he knows best. But it may be said with confidence that a great republic will always be exposed to far greater perils than a small one.

problem: 'the dejection of wretchedness' rendered 'the despair of poverty' (different word and sense).
replacement: All the passions most fatal to republican institutions spread as territory grows, while the virtues that maintain their dignity do not grow in the same proportion. The ambition of the citizens increases with the power of the State, and the strength of parties with the importance of the ends they have in view. But devotion to the common good, which is the surest check on destructive passions, is no stronger in a large republic than in a small one. Indeed, it could easily be proved that it is weaker and less sincere. The arrogance of wealth and the dejection of the wretched, capital cities of unusual size, a lax morality, a vulgar selfishness, and a great confusion of interests — these are the dangers that almost invariably arise from the great size of States. But several of these evils are hardly harmful to a monarchy, and some of them help to maintain it. In monarchical States the strength of the government is its own; it may use the community, but it does not depend on it, and the authority of the prince is proportioned to the prosperity of the nation. But the only security a republican government has against these evils lies in the support of the majority. This support is not proportionally greater in a large republic than in a small one. So while the means of attack constantly increase in both number and influence, the power of resistance remains the same, or rather it may be said to diminish, since the inclinations and interests of the people become more varied as the population grows, and the difficulty of forming a solid majority keeps increasing. It has also been observed that the intensity of human passions is heightened not only by the importance of the end they aim at but by the number of individuals who are moved by them at the same time. Everyone has had occasion to notice that his emotions in the midst of a sympathetic crowd are far greater than those he would have felt alone. In great republics the force of political passion is irresistible, not only because it aims at gigantic purposes, but because it is felt and shared by millions of men at the same time.

problem: 'abstract of the patriotic zeal' rendered 'sum' (epitome, not aggregate).
replacement: It is beyond dispute that the love and the habits of republican government in the United States were produced in the townships and in the provincial assemblies. In a small State like Connecticut, for instance, cutting a canal or building a road is a weighty political question. The State has no army to pay and no wars to wage, and it cannot bestow much wealth or honor on its leading citizens. In such a State no form of government could be more natural or more suitable than a republic. But it is this same republican spirit, these manners and customs of a free people, produced and nurtured in the different States, that are afterward applied to the country at large. The public spirit of the Union is, so to speak, nothing more than a summary of the patriotic zeal of the provinces. Every citizen of the United States transfers his attachment to his little republic into the common store of American patriotism. In defending the Union he defends the growing prosperity of his own district, the right to conduct its affairs, and the hope of getting improvements adopted that may favor his own interest. These are motives that move men more readily than the general interests of the country and the glory of the nation.

problem: 'manners' left unmodernized (mores); 'Even then' adds a concessive turn not in the source.
replacement: On the other hand, if the temper and the customs of the inhabitants especially fitted them to promote the welfare of a great republic, the Federal system cleared away the obstacles they might have met. The confederation of all the American States has none of the ordinary disadvantages that result from great concentrations of people. The Union is a great republic in size, but the small number of objects its government provides for makes it resemble a small State. Its acts are important, but they are rare. Because the sovereignty of the Union is limited and incomplete, its exercise is not incompatible with liberty, for it does not excite those insatiable desires for fame and power that have proved so fatal to great republics. Because the country has no common center, vast capital cities, colossal wealth, abject poverty, and sudden revolutions are all unknown. Political passion, instead of sweeping over the land like a torrent of desolation, spends its strength against the interests and individual passions of each State.

problem: General statement turned into a hypothetical ('Suppose'); 'manners' left unmodernized.
replacement: When a legislator succeeds, after persistent efforts, in exerting an indirect influence on the destiny of nations, mankind praises his genius. But in fact the geographical position of the country, which he cannot change, a social condition that arose without his help, customs and opinions whose source he cannot trace, and an origin he does not know all exercise such an irresistible influence over the course of society that he himself is carried away by the current after a futile resistance. Like the navigator, he may steer the vessel that carries him along, but he can neither change its structure, nor raise the winds, nor calm the waters that swell beneath him.

problem: Hedge and logic lost: source says he scarcely ever met a citizen who could not distinguish the laws AND who, after separating the matters, could not point out the jurisdictions. Candidate turns the second part into a flat positive claim ('he could point out').
replacement: Once the general theory is understood, countless difficulties remain to be solved in applying it. The sovereignty of the Union is so entangled with that of the States that it is impossible to see its boundaries at first glance. The whole structure of the government is artificial and conventional. It would be poorly suited to a people that has not long been accustomed to conducting its own affairs, or to one in which the science of politics has not reached the humblest classes of society. I have never been more struck by the good sense and practical judgment of the Americans than in the ingenious devices by which they get around the countless difficulties arising from their Federal Constitution. I have scarcely ever met a plain American citizen who could not distinguish, with surprising ease, the obligations created by the laws of Congress from those created by the laws of his own State, or who, after separating the matters that fall under the authority of the Union from those the local legislature is competent to regulate, could not point out the exact limits of the several jurisdictions of the Federal courts and the tribunals of the State.

problem: Source's 'consequently' (inference) replaced by 'and yet' (concession), changing the logical connective.
replacement: One of the circumstances that most powerfully helps to support the Federal government in America is that the States have not only similar interests, a common origin, and a common tongue, but have also reached the same stage of civilization, which almost always makes a union workable. I know of no European nation, however small, that shows less uniformity among its different provinces than the American people, who occupy a territory as large as half of Europe. The distance from Maine to Georgia is reckoned at about one thousand miles, but the difference between the civilization of Maine and that of Georgia is slighter than the difference between the habits of Normandy and those of Brittany. Maine and Georgia are at the opposite ends of a great empire, and they therefore have by nature more real inducements to form a confederation than Normandy and Brittany, which are separated only by a bridge.
